issues.title: [Bug] CPU FP8 `scaled_mm` produces NaN under torch.compile with zero-dim tensor
issues.author: XAheli
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`test_zero_dim_tensorwise` fails on CPU when `which_dim_zero=1` and `use_torch_compile=True`. The FP8 `scaled_mm` path produces NaN values (22.1% element mismatch) instead of matching the eager result.

The CUDA variant of this issue was fixed in #183964 (which resolved #175206), but the CPU path appears to have the same underlying bug. The fix likely only addressed the CUDA/inductor codegen path and missed the CPU FP8 emulation kernel.

### Reproduction

```bash
python test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py TestFP8MatmulCPU.test_zero_dim_tensorwise_which_dim_zero_1_use_torch_compile_True_cpu
```

### Error

```
FAIL: test_zero_dim_tensorwise_which_dim_zero_1_use_torch_compile_True_cpu

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test/test_scaled_matmul_cuda.py", line 1937, in test_zero_dim_tensorwise
    self.assertEqual(out_fp32, out_fp8.to(torch.float))
AssertionError: Tensor-likes are not close!

Mismatched elements: 226 / 1024 (22.1%)
Greatest absolute difference: nan at index (0, 18) (up to 1e-05 allowed)
Greatest relative difference: nan at index (0, 18) (up to 1.3e-06 allowed)
```

### Environment

- PyTorch: 2.14.0a0+gitac94967 (built from source, upstream/main)
- Python: 3.11.15
- Hardware: NVIDIA H200, tested on CPU path
- OS: Linux (RHEL-based)

### Context

- The test was introduced in #164266 (split scaled-mm tests into separate file)
- #175206 reported a similar CUDA regression with mixed scalar/single-element scale shapes under `torch.compile`
- #183964 fixed the CUDA variant by normalizing tensorwise scales before template config generation
- Only the `torch.compile=True` + `which_dim_zero=1` combination fails; eager mode and `which_dim_zero=0` pass fine

issues.author: rYm-A

### 🐛 Describe the bug

The presence of larger dimension size of 255 in the operator torch.eye causes an error during the code generation in Inductor: the Metal code cannot be generated from the scheduled kernel. 

The error seems to point to [this dictionary](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/dc1c3dfd991f182532c0b434e73f07736d78d6eb/torch/_inductor/codegen/mps.py#L42), where the torch.uint16 data type is not included. @malfet is there a reason why is this type not included if it's supported according the [documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/mtldatatype/ushort)?

Repro:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from typing import Tuple

class OnlyEye(nn.Module):

    def forward(self, x0: torch.Tensor, Xi: torch.Tensor) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        I = torch.eye(Xi.shape[-1], dtype=Xi.dtype, device=Xi.device)
        sol = Xi + 1
        err = torch.matmul(Xi, I)

        return sol, err

device = torch.device("mps")
x = torch.zeros(S, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
Xi = torch.zeros(10, S, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)

model = OnlyEye().eval().to(device)
compiled = torch.compile(model)
with torch.inference_mode():

```

issues.title: [Inductor] as_strided_ metadata mutation is not reflected on original tensor
issues.author: rookieLiu2018
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.Tensor.as_strided_` mutates the size/stride metadata of the original tensor in eager mode. However, after compiling the same function with `torch.compile(..., backend="inductor", fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)`, the returned view has the expected metadata, but the original tensor's metadata remains stale.

In the repro below, eager mode shows that both `x` and `y` have size `(2, 2)` and stride `(2, 1)` after:

```python
y = x.as_strided_((2, 2), (2, 1))
```

However, the compiled path returns:

```text
x.size()   == (4,)
x.stride() == (1,)
```

while `y.size()` and `y.stride()` are correctly `(2, 2)` and `(2, 1)`.

This looks like an Inductor metadata visibility / mutation semantics issue: the `as_strided_` mutation is reflected on the returned tensor `y`, but not on the original tensor `x`.

Expected behavior: compiled execution should match eager. After `as_strided_`, both `x` and `y` should expose the mutated size/stride metadata.

Actual behavior: compiled execution leaves `x.size()` and `x.stride()` stale.

```python
import torch

def fn():
    x = torch.arange(4.0, dtype=torch.float32)
    y = x.as_strided_((2, 2), (2, 1))
    observer = torch.max(y)
    return y, x.size(), y.size(), x.stride(), y.stride(), observer

def show(name, out):
    y, x_size, y_size, x_stride, y_stride, observer = out
    print(name)
    print("y:", y)
    print("x_size:", tuple(x_size))
    print("y_size:", tuple(y_size))
    print("x_stride:", tuple(x_stride))
    print("y_stride:", tuple(y_stride))
    print("max:", observer)

print("torch", torch.__version__)

eager = fn()
show("eager", eager)

compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)
compiled_out = compiled()
show("compiled", compiled_out)
```

Observed output:

```text
torch 2.10.0+cpu
eager
y: tensor([[0., 1.],
        [2., 3.]])
x_size: (2, 2)
y_size: (2, 2)
x_stride: (2, 1)
y_stride: (2, 1)
max: tensor(3.)
compiled
y: tensor([[0., 1.],
        [2., 3.]])
x_size: (4,)
y_size: (2, 2)
x_stride: (1,)
y_stride: (2, 1)
max: tensor(3.)
```

This is not a numerical tolerance issue. The tensor values and `torch.max(y)` match, but the structure/metadata visible through `x.size()` and `x.stride()` differs between eager and compiled execution after the in-place metadata mutation.


### Versions

`Pytotch Version: 2.10.0+cpu`

issues.title: [inductor] Upsample(mode='area') fails under torch.compile(dynamic=True) — "cannot determine truth value of Relational" in _adaptive_avg_pool2d lowering
issues.author: lijunqiang123
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2, mode='area')` (which decomposes to `aten._adaptive_avg_pool2d` ) crashes under `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` . Inductor's `_adaptive_avg_pool2d` lowering contains a static if `window_size > 25`: branch that cannot be resolved when window_size is a symbolic expression under `dynamic=True` .

Eager mode works correctly.

### Minimal repro 
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

x = torch.randn(1, 3, 15, 19)
m = nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2, mode='area')
m = torch.compile(m, dynamic=True)
m(x)    #crash here!
```
### Error logs
```
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: LoweringException: TypeError: cannot determine truth 
value of Relational: (((2*TruncToInt(2.0*ToFloat(s69)) + 13)//(TruncToInt(2.0*ToFloat(
s69)))))*(((2*TruncToInt(2.0*ToFloat(s87)) + 17)//(TruncToInt(2.0*ToFloat(s87))))) > 25
  target: aten._adaptive_avg_pool2d.default
  args[0]: TensorBox(StorageBox(
    InputBuffer(name='arg3_1', layout=FixedLayout('cpu', torch.float32, size=[1, s50, s69, s87],
    stride=[s50*s69*s87, s69*s87, s87, 1]))
  ))
  args[1]: [TruncToInt(2.0*ToFloat(s69)), TruncToInt(2.0*ToFloat(s87))]

  File "torch/_inductor/lowering.py", line 5831, in _adaptive_avg_pool2d
    if window_size > 25:
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "sympy/core/relational.py", line 519, in __bool__
    raise TypeError(...)
```
### Root cause
In `torch/_inductor/lowering.py:5831` , `_adaptive_avg_pool2d` lowering uses a static Python `if` to choose between kernel implementations:

```
if window_size > 25:
    # one kernel path
else:
    # another kernel path
```

`Upsample(mode='area')` decomposes to `aten._adaptive_avg_pool2d` . When `dynamic=True` , `window_size` is a symbolic expression (SymInt / SymPy object), and `window_size > 25` returns a `Relational` object instead of `bool` — causing SymPy to refuse evaluation.

### Possible fix
1. Guard on concrete values: insert `torch._check(window_size > 25)` prior to the static if
2. Use `torch._sympy.definitely_true() / torch._sympy.could_be_true()` to branch with symbolic awareness
3. Emit a conditional kernel dispatch that resolves at runtime


### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.13.0.dev20260521+cu126
OS: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Python: 3.12
CUDA: 12.6
```

issues.title: [dynamo] [dynamic] `nn.LazyLinear` reject SymInt when direct using `torch.compile()`
issues.author: shaoyuyoung
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch._inductor import config

config.fallback_random = True
torch.set_grad_enabled(False)
torch._dynamo.config.capture_scalar_outputs = True

class Model(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.lazy_fc = nn.LazyLinear(out_features=128)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.lazy_fc(x)
        return x


model = Model()


x = torch.randn(1, 28, 28)

inputs = [x]

device = "cpu"
def run_test(model, inputs, device, backend):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model.to(device)
    inputs = [input.to(device) for input in inputs]
    if backend != "eager":
        model = torch.compile(model, backend=backend, dynamic=True)
    try:
        output = model(*inputs)
        print(f"succeed on {backend}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(e)

run_test(model, inputs, device, 'aot_eager')
run_test(model, inputs, device, 'eager')


```

If we first use eager to initialize lazylinear (i.e., swap the position of the last two lines of code), dynamo can catch `in_features` and run successfully.

### Error logs

```
RuntimeError: /pytorch/build/aten/src/ATen/RegisterCPU_1.cpp:2512: SymIntArrayRef expected to contain only concrete integers
succeed on eager
```

### Versions

2.10.0.dev20251103+cu126

issues.title: [Dynamo] Architectural Improvement: Trace-time detection for in-place rank mutation on placeholders
issues.author: P1yansh
issues.body:
**Context:**
This issue tracks a future architectural improvement following the fix for internal crash #185888 (in-place rank mutation via `as_strided_` under dynamic shapes). 

Currently, Dynamo allows `FakeTensor`s to mutate their rank in-place during tracing if the user calls an op like `x.as_strided_((2, 2), (2, 1))` on a 1D input. Dynamo only catches this at the very end of compilation during guard generation in `symbolic_shapes.py`, where it raises `Unsupported` and triggers a graph break. 

While the guard-time fix prevents compiler crashes and silent correctness bugs, it is suboptimal because it allows an invalid state (a mutated placeholder rank) to exist inside the tracing machinery for a brief window.

**The Architectural Goal:**
The ideal fix is to intercept this mutation at the exact millisecond it occurs—during `FakeTensor` dispatch in `torch/_subclasses/fake_tensor.py`. If an in-place metadata-mutating op is called on a tensor that is a Dynamo graph input, Dynamo should immediately trigger a graph break.

**Benefits of Trace-Time Detection:**
1. **Protecting Compiler Invariants:** Prevents invalid IR (mutated placeholder rank) from flowing through downstream FX passes and shape analysis.
2. **Failing Fast:** Avoids wasting compilation time tracing the rest of a model that is ultimately going to be discarded.
3. **Accurate Error Localization:** Allows Dynamo to point the user to the exact line of Python code that caused the graph break, rather than a generic "ambient guard" failure.

**The Challenge:**
`FakeTensor` is a low-level primitive used by many PyTorch subsystems (`torch.export`, `torch.jit.trace`, FSDP, etc.). Hardcoding a check like `if tensor.is_dynamo_placeholder` inside `fake_tensor.py` would cross a delicate boundary between the eager subsystem (`torch._subclasses`) and the compiler subsystem (`torch._dynamo`), creating coupling and circular import risks.

**Proposed Direction:**
Instead of direct coupling, we should use an inversion of control. `FakeTensorMode` could expose generic metadata-mutation hooks. Dynamo could register a listener during tracing that catches these mutations, checks if the tensor is a tracked placeholder, and raises `Unsupported` right then and there.

**Related PRs:**
* Pending PR for guard-time fix in #185888

issues.title: [MPS] Compiled training is 4x slower than eager because layout optimization forces channels_last
issues.author: eyupcanakman
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Training a small conv net on MPS with torch.compile runs 4.5x slower than eager on the current nightly, and 9x slower on the 2.13.0 release wheel.
There are zero graph breaks.
The cause is inductor's layout optimization, and setting `TORCHINDUCTOR_LAYOUT_OPTIMIZATION=0` turns compile into a win at every shape I tried.
I tracked it down with Claude's help and reviewed everything below.
The numbers are from my machine.

Repro, batch 256 at 32x32, bf16 autocast, Apple M5 Pro, macOS 27.

```python
import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c_in, c_out, stride=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, stride, 1, bias=False)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 3, 1, 1, bias=False)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out)
        self.short = (
            nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 1, stride, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out))
            if stride != 1 or c_in != c_out
            else nn.Identity()
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        out = torch.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out))
        return torch.relu(out + self.short(x))


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, w=24):
        super().__init__()
        self.stem = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, w, 3, 1, 1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(w), nn.ReLU())
        self.stage1 = Block(w, w)
        self.stage2 = nn.Sequential(Block(w, 2 * w, 2), Block(2 * w, 2 * w))
        self.stage3 = nn.Sequential(Block(2 * w, 4 * w, 2), Block(4 * w, 4 * w))
        self.head = nn.Linear(4 * w, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.stage3(self.stage2(self.stage1(self.stem(x))))
        return self.head(x.mean(dim=(2, 3)))


dev = torch.device("mps")


def bench(compiled, iters=15):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m = Net().to(dev)
    if compiled:
        m.compile()
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9)
    lf = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    x = torch.randn(256, 3, 32, 32, device=dev)
    y = torch.randint(0, 10, (256,), device=dev)

    def step():
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        with torch.autocast("mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
            loss = lf(m(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

    for i in range(iters + 5):
        if i == 5:
            torch.mps.synchronize()
            t = time.time()
        step()
    torch.mps.synchronize()
    return (time.time() - t) / iters * 1000


e = bench(False)
c = bench(True)
print(f"torch {torch.__version__}")
print(f"eager:    {e:7.2f} ms/step")
print(f"compiled: {c:7.2f} ms/step   ({c / e:.2f}x eager)")
```

Output.

```
torch 2.14.0.dev20260807
eager:      25.59 ms/step
compiled:  114.48 ms/step   (4.47x eager)
```

Same model swept across input shapes, eager -> compiled ms/step, with layout optimization on (default) and off (`TORCHINDUCTOR_LAYOUT_OPTIMIZATION=0`), each config in a fresh process and cache.

```
                 layout opt on (default)      TORCHINDUCTOR_LAYOUT_OPTIMIZATION=0
8x8   b256     7.20 ->   9.87   1.37x           7.18 ->  5.58   0.78x
16x16 b256     8.81 ->  31.65   3.59x           7.96 ->  6.75   0.85x
24x24 b128     8.46 ->  35.19   4.16x           8.42 ->  7.11   0.84x
32x32 b128    13.92 ->  60.50   4.35x          13.75 -> 11.95   0.87x
32x32 b256    27.36 -> 119.08   4.35x          27.38 -> 19.78   0.72x
```

With the flag, compiled is faster than eager at every shape.
The regression grows with spatial size, which matches the per-op numbers below.

AI-assisted analysis (Claude), reviewed by me:

`decide_layout_opt` in `torch/_inductor/graph.py` enables channels_last for graphs with convolutions, and `aten.convolution_backward` on MPS runs about 10x slower on channels_last inputs than on contiguous ones at common shapes, so the compiled backward pays that penalty 13 times per step.
With `backend="eager"` the step takes 27.0 ms and with `backend="aot_eager"` 26.5 ms, both matching eager, so the loss is inside inductor codegen rather than dynamo or AOTAutograd.
Timing every call in the generated backward code, with a sync around each call, attributes 84% of the backward to the 13 external `convolution_backward` calls at 8.3 ms per call, while no generated Metal kernel exceeds 1.3 ms.
The op on its own shows the layout penalty in bf16.

```
convolution_backward (256,24,32,32) w=(24,24,3,3)  contiguous 1.84 ms   channels_last 23.52 ms   12.8x
convolution_backward (256,48,16,16) w=(48,48,3,3)  contiguous 0.53 ms   channels_last  5.74 ms   10.9x
convolution_backward (256,96,8,8)   w=(96,96,5,5)  contiguous 1.92 ms   channels_last  3.86 ms    2.0x
```

Forward convolution is unaffected and is even faster on channels_last at these shapes (0.48 ms vs 0.94 ms at 32x32), so inference would not notice.

The heuristics in `decide_layout_opt` come from CUDA benchmarks (the code carries a `TODO - get different values per hardware`) and the function has no MPS branch.
The channels_last penalty inside MPS `convolution_backward` itself may deserve its own look, since it grows with spatial size.

End of the AI-assisted analysis.
I patched `decide_layout_opt` locally to skip layout optimization for MPS training graphs and compiled training went from 4.5x slower to 1.3x faster than eager.
I can send that patch if it is the right direction.

For reference, #150121 tracks compile on MPS but has no conv training performance item, and #189239 is the mirror problem on CUDA and XPU where backward graphs get too little channels_last rather than too much.

### Versions

```

ROCM used to build PyTorch: N/A
OS: macOS 27.0 (arm64)

```
import time
import torch


WARMUP = 50
ITERATIONS = 200
INPUT_SHAPE = (256, 24, 32, 32)
WEIGHT_SHAPE = (24, 24, 3, 3)


def benchmark(memory_format):
    x = torch.randn(INPUT_SHAPE, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    grad_output = torch.randn(INPUT_SHAPE, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    weight = torch.randn(WEIGHT_SHAPE, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

    weight = weight.contiguous(memory_format=memory_format)

    def grad_weight():
        return torch.ops.aten.convolution_backward.default(
            grad_output,
            x,
            weight,
            None,
            (1, 1),
            (1, 1),
            (1, 1),
            False,

            1,
            (False, True, False),

    torch.mps.synchronize()

    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(ITERATIONS):

    torch.mps.synchronize()

issues.title: torch.compile peak-memory reordering changes native_dropout RNG order when fallback_random=True
issues.author: O1range
issues.body:
## Summary

When both of the following Inductor options are enabled:

```python
torch._inductor.config.fallback_random = True
torch._inductor.config.reorder_for_peak_memory = True
```

`torch.compile` may reorder independent `aten.native_dropout` calls. The fallback operator consumes the global RNG state, but the scheduler does not see this hidden state dependency. Consequently, the same dropout calls receive different random masks in eager and compiled execution even when `torch.manual_seed()` is reset to the same value immediately before each run.

In the reproducer below, eager executes the large encoder branch first and the small decoder branch last. Inductor's peak-memory scheduling moves the decoder branch first. This changes both the output and gradients.

## Environment

```text
PyTorch: 2.12.0+cpu
Git revision: 7661cd9c6b841b62b7f411aa52ec51f05457263b
Python: 3.10
Device: CPU
```

## Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile


torch._inductor.config.fallback_random = True
torch._inductor.config.reorder_for_peak_memory = True


def model(encoder, decoder):
    # The branches are independent until the final add. A sufficiently large
    # graph causes peak-memory scheduling to move the small branch first.
    for _ in range(17):
        encoder = F.dropout(F.relu(encoder), p=0.5, training=True)
    decoder = F.dropout(decoder, p=0.5, training=True)
    return encoder + decoder


def run(fn, encoder, decoder):
    torch.manual_seed(2026)
    with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU], record_shapes=True) as prof:
        output = fn(encoder, decoder)

    dropout_shapes = [
        tuple(event.input_shapes[0])
        for event in prof.events()
        if event.name in {"aten::dropout", "aten::native_dropout"}
        and event.input_shapes
    ]
    order = [
        "decoder" if shape == (1, 1, 64) else "encoder"
        for shape in dropout_shapes
    ]
    return output, order


# requires_grad=True selects the training graph. Calling backward is not needed
# to expose the forward RNG-order mismatch.
encoder = torch.randn(1, 128, 64, requires_grad=True)
decoder = torch.randn(1, 1, 64, requires_grad=True)
compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
compiled_model(encoder, decoder)  # compile outside the profiler

eager_output, eager_order = run(model, encoder, decoder)
compiled_output, compiled_order = run(compiled_model, encoder, decoder)

print("eager order:  ", eager_order)
print("compiled order:", compiled_order)
print("outputs equal:", torch.equal(eager_output, compiled_output))

torch.testing.assert_close(compiled_output, eager_output, rtol=0, atol=0)
```

Run with:

```bash
python debug_dropout_cpu.py
```

## Actual behavior

Abbreviated output:

```text
eager order:    [encoder x17, decoder]
compiled order: [decoder, encoder x17]
outputs equal: False

AssertionError: Tensor-likes are not equal!
```

## Expected behavior

With the same input tensors and manual seed, `torch.compile` should preserve the observable RNG ordering of fallback random operators. The compiled order should be `[encoder x17, decoder]`, and the output should exactly equal eager output.

## Root cause

The relevant path in the inspected source is:

```text
torch/_inductor/lowering.py
  native_dropout()
    fallback_random=True
      -> ir.FallbackKernel.create(aten.native_dropout.default, ...)

torch/_inductor/scheduler.py
  Scheduler initialization
    reorder_for_peak_memory=True
      -> memory.reorder_for_peak_memory(...)
```

The encoder and decoder are independent dataflow branches until the final add. Therefore, moving the decoder branch before the encoder is a valid topological reordering if `native_dropout` is treated as a pure operator.

However, fallback `native_dropout` consumes the global CPU RNG state. The actual semantic dependency is:

```text
RNG S0 -> encoder dropout 0 -> S1 -> ... -> encoder dropout 16 -> S17
        -> decoder dropout -> S18
```

That dependency is absent from the scheduler graph. Peak-memory scheduling can therefore move the small decoder branch first and assign every dropout a different part of the global random-number sequence.

Registering `aten.native_dropout.default` as an `ORDERED` effect makes AOTAutograd thread an effect token through the calls. Inductor lowers `with_effects` by adding ordering dependencies between the generated operations, which prevents the peak-memory scheduler from reversing them.

## Proposed fix: opt-in config switch

Add an option for users/backends that require eager RNG order for fallback dropout. The default remains `False`, so this has no behavior change unless the option is explicitly enabled.

### `torch/_inductor/config.py`

```diff
 # fallback to eager for random/dropout, this is slow but useful for debugging
 fallback_random = False

+# Preserve eager RNG ordering for fallback native_dropout calls by threading an
+# ordered effect token through the compiled graph.
+preserve_fallback_random_order = False
```

### `torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py`

Add this context manager immediately before `_compile_fx_main`:

```diff
+@contextlib.contextmanager
+def _preserve_fallback_random_order():
+    if not (
+        config.fallback_random
+        and config.preserve_fallback_random_order
+    ):
+        yield
+        return
+
+    from torch._higher_order_ops.effects import (
+        _EffectType,
+        _register_effectful_op,
+    )
+
+    handle = _register_effectful_op(
+        torch.ops.aten.native_dropout.default,
+        _EffectType.ORDERED,
+    )
+    try:
+        yield
+    finally:
+        handle.destroy()
```

Enter the context before AOTAutograd traces the graph:

```diff
 def _compile_fx_main(...):
     ...
     with (
+        _preserve_fallback_random_order(),
         _use_lazy_graph_module(dynamo_config.use_lazy_graph_module),
         enable_python_dispatcher(),
         ...
     ):
```

Enable it with:

```python
torch._inductor.config.fallback_random = True
torch._inductor.config.preserve_fallback_random_order = True
```

### Verification result

```text
switch=False:
  eager:    [encoder x17, decoder]
  compiled: [decoder, encoder x17]
  outputs equal: False

switch=True:
  eager:    [encoder x17, decoder]
  compiled: [encoder x17, decoder]
  outputs equal: True
```

### Trade-offs

- No default behavior or performance change.
- Users must know that the switch is required for correct fallback RNG ordering.
- The effect registry is process-global. Temporarily changing it during a scoped config patch can race with concurrent compilation in another thread. A production implementation may need a non-global conditional effect mechanism or compiler-level dependency representation.
- Preserving order may reduce peak-memory scheduling freedom for graphs containing many fallback dropout calls. Because the new switch defaults to `False`, users opt into this correctness/performance trade-off explicitly.

The current local PyTorch 2.12 source contains this switch-based implementation.

## Verification matrix

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Original 2.12, `fallback_random=True` | Reproduced order and output mismatch |
| New switch off | Mismatch remains; existing behavior is unchanged |
| New switch on | Dropout order and output match eager |
| New switch on with backward | Encoder and decoder gradients match eager |

issues.title: aot_export_joint_with_descriptors don't work  with compile inside due to dynamo config
issues.author: tugsbayasgalan
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python 
from torch.nn.attention.flex_attention import create_block_mask, flex_attention
import torch 

class MixedFakeModeModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim=64, use_inductor=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.dim = dim
        self.q_proj = torch.nn.Linear(64, 64)
        self.k_proj = torch.nn.Linear(64, 64)
        self.v_proj = torch.nn.Linear(64, 64)
        self.use_inductor = use_inductor
        self.flex_attention = torch.compile(flex_attention, backend="inductor")

    def forward(self, x):
        batch_size, seq_len, _ = x.shape

        # Process input first - this creates fake tensors in export's fake mode
        processed = self.q_proj(x)

        # Create some computation that depends on processed tensor
        intermediate = processed.sum(dim=-1).detach()  # Shape: (batch, seq_len)

        # Now call create_block_mask which internally calls torch.compile
        # The mask function will capture 'intermediate' which is a fake tensor
        # from export's fake mode, but create_block_mask will create its own fake mode
        def dynamic_mask_function(batch_idx, head_idx, q_idx, kv_idx):
            # This captures the intermediate tensor from the outer scope
            # When torch.compile is called inside create_block_mask,
            # this tensor will be from export's fake mode while new tensors
            # created inside will be from the nested fake mode
            threshold = intermediate[
                batch_idx, q_idx % seq_len
            ]  # Access the captured tensor
            return (kv_idx <= q_idx) & (threshold > 0)  # Mix fake modes

        block_mask = create_block_mask(
            mask_mod=dynamic_mask_function,
            B=batch_size,
            H=None,
            Q_LEN=seq_len,
            KV_LEN=seq_len,
            device=x.device,
        )
        q = self.q_proj(processed).view(batch_size, 1, seq_len, self.dim)
        k = self.k_proj(processed).view(batch_size, 1, seq_len, self.dim)
        v = self.v_proj(processed).view(batch_size, 1, seq_len, self.dim)

        # Use flex_attention with torch.compile - during export, compile should be skipped
        backend = "inductor" if self.use_inductor else "eager"
        out = self.flex_attention(
            q, k, v, block_mask=block_mask
        )

        return out

model = MixedFakeModeModel(use_inductor=True)
x = torch.randn(2, 128, 64)
from torch._functorch.aot_autograd import aot_export_joint_with_descriptors
from contextlib import ExitStack
aot_export_joint_with_descriptors(ExitStack(), model, (x,))

```
Errors with:
```
RuntimeError: Detected that you are using FX to symbolically trace a dynamo-optimized function. This is not supported at the moment.
```

non-strict export doesn't error btw. We can probably copy paste whatever we do for non-strict here. 

### Versions

main

issues.title: [inductor] schedule_overlap_bucketing crashes with AttributeError when both memory caps are None (the documented "no limit" configuration)
issues.author: X-XG
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`schedule_overlap_bucketing` documents its memory caps as optional:

```
max_memory_increase_gb: Maximum GB increase above baseline memory (absolute cap). If None, no absolute limit.
max_memory_increase_ratio: Maximum increase as ratio of baseline peak memory. If None, no ratio limit.
```

Passing both as `None` — the documented "no limits" configuration — crashes on
the very first scheduled node:

```
File "torch/_inductor/fx_passes/overlap_scheduling.py", line 1140, in _schedule
    self.memory_tracker.schedule_node(node)
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'schedule_node'
```

### Repro (single process, CPU, no GPU needed)

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.fx.experimental.proxy_tensor import make_fx
from torch.testing._internal.distributed.fake_pg import FakeStore

dist.init_process_group("fake", rank=0, world_size=4, store=FakeStore())
group_name = dist.distributed_c10d._get_default_group().group_name


def f(x, w):
    ag = torch.ops._c10d_functional.all_gather_into_tensor(x, 4, group_name)
    ag = torch.ops._c10d_functional.wait_tensor(ag)
    return ag @ w


gm = make_fx(f, tracing_mode="fake")(torch.randn(8, 16), torch.randn(16, 16))

from torch._inductor.fx_passes.overlap_scheduling import schedule_overlap_bucketing

schedule_overlap_bucketing(
    gm,
    max_memory_increase_gb=None,
    max_memory_increase_ratio=None,
)
```

### Analysis

In `OverlapScheduler.__init__`:

```python
needs_memory_tracking = (
    max_memory_increase_gb is not None or max_memory_increase_ratio is not None
)
if needs_memory_tracking:
    ...
    self.memory_tracker = MemoryTracker(self.graph)
else:
    ...
    self.memory_tracker = None  # type: ignore[assignment]
```

but the base class dereferences `self.memory_tracker` unconditionally in six
places (line numbers for 2.14.0.dev20260728):

| line | method | expression |
|---|---|---|
| 643 | `_prefetch_would_exceed_memory_budget` | `.current_memory_bytes + size` |
| 935 | `_get_next_nodes` | `.current_memory_bytes` |
| 1140 | `_schedule` | `.schedule_node(node)` (first hit) |
| 1145 | `_schedule` | `.get_current_memory_bytes()` |
| 1616 | `_reorder_graph` | `.peak_memory` |
| 1627 | `_reorder_graph` | `.peak_memory` |

The `None` branch was introduced for `ManualOverlapScheduler`
(#183565, "Skip MemoryTracker in ManualOverlapScheduler"), which overrides the
scheduling loop; for the base `OverlapScheduler` the branch is unreachable
without crashing, and no test exercises it — the `# type: ignore[assignment]`
on a non-Optional attribute is the tell.

### Suggested fix

Guard the six call sites (`if self.memory_tracker is not None`), or install a
no-op tracker when both caps are `None`, mirroring how
`ManualOverlapScheduler` sidesteps it.

### Versions

torch 2.14.0.dev20260728+cu130; per file history the code is unchanged on
current `main`.


cc @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo

comments.author: HussainNizamani
comments.body:
Reproduced on current main (Linux aarch64, CPU-only build). With both memory caps set to `None` the pass crashes exactly as reported:

`overlap_scheduling.py:1140` -`AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'schedule_node'`

The cause is right there in the source: the no-limits branch sets `self.memory_tracker = None` (around line 531), but `_schedule` and five other places (643, 935, 1145, 1616, 1627) call it without checking.
